 Notorious Mexican drug lord, who was convicted of killing US DEA agent, dies at 80
 Story by Reuters 
 Updated Nov 15, 2026, 8:03 PM ET 
 PUBLISHED Nov 15, 2026, 6:37 PM ET

 Flor Cordero/Reuters/File

 Mexico City Reuters  —  
 Miguel Ángel Félix Gallardo, founder of one of Mexico’s first major drug cartels whose conviction for the 1985 killing of a US drug-enforcement agent made him one of the country’s most notorious traffickers, died in hospital on Sunday at age 80.
 Local security authorities said Félix Gallardo was transferred to a private hospital in the western city of Guadalajara two days ago but suffered multiple organ failure and died around 2 p.m. on Sunday.
 Imprisoned since 1989, Félix Gallardo was an inmate in a maximum-security prison in western Jalisco state, though his lawyers repeatedly sought house arrest on the grounds of his deteriorating health.
 Rising to prominence in the 1970s, the former cartel kingpin was an architect of Mexico’s modern drug-trafficking trade, igniting a series of turf wars that have led to hundreds of thousands of deaths and disappearances in ensuing decades.
 His rise and fall was portrayed on screen by Mexican actor Diego Luna in the 2018 hit Netflix series “Narcos: Mexico.”
 Related article
 A view shows the building where authorities said they found a suspected illegal cryptocurrency mining operation that was allegedly drawing power from infrastructure linked to a nearby hydroelectric system, in Tlaola, Puebla state, Mexico, September 8, 2026. REUTERS/Daniel Becerril 
 Daniel Becerril/Reuters 
 Hidden crypto farm in Mexican mountains puts spotlight on cartel funding 
 4 min read 
 Born in 1946 in Culiacan, Sinaloa, a northwestern state that would later become synonymous with narco-trafficking, he worked as a police officer and bodyguard for a local governor then became a powerful criminal capo known as the “boss of bosses.”
 Félix Gallardo and others set up the cartel in Guadalajara, the Jalisco state capital and a fast-growing economic powerhouse, becoming the first to move cocaine to the US on a massive scale and to forge an alliance with Colombian drug barons, including Pablo Escobar’s Medellin cartel.
 His narcotics empire expanded in the 1970s and 1980s thanks to bribes that won protection from corrupt officials and innovations like using light aircraft to move drugs across the continent, supported by fellow kingpins like Rafael Caro Quintero .
 A Jalisco State police officer stands guard in front of the Hospital Country 2000, where Mexican drug lord Miguel Ángel Félix Gallardo, aka "The Boss of Bosses," had been admitted in a health emergency in Guadalajara, Mexico on November 13. 
 Ulises Ruiz/AFP/Getty Images 
 His legal battles stretched across decades.
 Arrested in 1989, Félix Gallardo was sentenced to 40 years in prison on drug-trafficking and weapons charges tied to the Guadalajara cartel.
 While already incarcerated, he faced a separate prosecution over the 1985 kidnapping and murder of US Drug Enforcement Administration agent Enrique “Kiki” Camarena and Mexican pilot Alfredo Zavala Avelar.
 Camarena’s killing caused a diplomatic dispute with Washington, which pressed Mexico hard to arrest those involved.
 In 2017, a federal court found Félix Gallardo guilty in that case and imposed a further 37-year sentence. He denied responsibility for the killings.
 Félix Gallardo suffered poor health in his final years, and was blind in one eye, practically deaf and unable to walk on his own by the time Spanish-language US network Telemundo interviewed him in prison in 2021. He maintained his innocence.
 “Thirty-two years have passed… That’s an eternity for a man who did not commit any crime,” he said.
